title: The Permission Paradox
lines: The Permission Paradox examines ideas evaluated through categories built from the past.
It asks how institutions can test unfamiliar possibilities without rewarding persuasive speculation.
AI sharpens the problem when candidate novelty outpaces society's capacity to evaluate it.
The book proposes conditional review, bounded inquiry, and funding arrangements that purchase learning.
Readers gain a way to inspect this tension without dividing people into visionaries and fools.

title: Different directions of reasoning
lines: An innovator may reason backward from a possible future that an institution cannot yet observe.
An evaluator usually reasons forward from existing evidence, precedent, and recognized categories.
Both approaches can be reasonable while producing a persistent mismatch.
The book also recognizes that an unfamiliar idea may simply be wrong.
Its question is how to distinguish responsible testing from either premature rejection or technological credulity.

title: A small test can teach
lines: Longview is the book's proposed approach to conditional assessment of future potential.
An idea could remain poorly evidenced yet justify a bounded, informative experiment.
Reversibility, meaningful benefit, protected participants, and learning value remain important conditions.
The funding discussion connects short experimental cycles with patience for difficult research.
These are institutional proposals to investigate, not automatic reasons to approve every unconventional claim.

title: Read the conditions for inquiry
lines: Begin with the mismatch between candidate novelty and the capacity to evaluate it.
Follow the review and funding proposals together, since each changes what the other can accomplish.
The book asks institutions to examine the costs of delay alongside the risks of action.
The Permission Paradox gives that tension a specific framework and a proposed research programme.
Read it to consider when a responsible experiment can teach more than another ranking.
